explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) comprises medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; crus cerebri is a midbrain component containing corticospinal tract fibers.
The brain stem proper consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; cerebellum and cerebral aqueduct are separate structures (cerebellum is hindbrain derivative, aqueduct is CSF space).
Cranial accessory nerve fibers arise from nucleus ambiguus in the medulla and join the vagus nerve, explaining why they are sometimes considered part of CN X.
The spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature sensation from the contralateral body side because second-order neurons cross at the spinal cord level before ascending.
Gracile and cuneate tracts receive blood from posterior spinal arteries and radicular arteries; all of the above (D) is correct since both sources contribute.
Lumbar puncture is performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace, below or above the tip of L4 spinous process, safely below the conus medullaris.
Complete transection above C5 results in quadriplegia because all descending motor pathways are interrupted before they branch to limb motor nuclei.
In hemisection, proprioception loss and UMN lesion findings are ipsilateral (A and B); pain/temperature loss is contralateral; A and B only is correct.
Brown-Sequard syndrome shows contralateral LMN lesion at same level - this is the exception; actually LMN at the level is ipsilateral, not contralateral.
UMN lesion produces spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign (E); hypotonia, wasting, restricted paralysis are LMN features not seen in UMN.
LMN lesion causes flaccid paralysis with marked muscle wasting; hypertonia, absent reflexes, increased reflexes, and Babinski are UMN features.
Syringomyelia first disrupts bilateral pain and temperature because the expanding syrinx damages crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure.
Crus cerebri is part of the cerebral peduncle in the midbrain, not the hindbrain; the rhombencephalon includes medulla, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle.
Brain stem includes midbrain, pons, and medulla; cerebellum is a separate hindbrain structure connected via cerebellar peduncles; cerebral aqueduct is ventriculwar space.
Cranial XI arises from nucleus ambiguus and travels with vagus nerve; this dual origin (spinal part from C1-C5) makes accessory nerve unique.
Spinal lemniscus is formed by crossed spinothalamic fibers carrying pain/temperature from the opposite side of the body after decussating at their entry level.
Dorsal column tracts are supplied by posterior spinal arteries (branches of vertebral artery) and radicular arteries from the aorta; all of these contribute.
The L4 spinous process tip is the standard landmark; needle is inserted at L3-L4 or L4-L5 level, below the conus medullaris ending at L1-L2.
Above C5 complete section causes quadriplegia (paralysis of all limbs) because corticospinal tracts to both upper and lower extremities are disrupted.
Hemisection produces ipsilateral proprioception loss and UMN signs below the lesion; A and B only captures both ipsilateral findings correctly.
Brown-Sequard has ipsilateral LMN at same level, not contralateral; this is the exception being tested; all other options describe true Brown-Sequard features.
Plantoflexion (E) describes normal reflex; UMN lesion causes Babinski (dorsiflexion), hypertonia, hyperreflexia, spasticity; other options describe LMN features.
Muscle wasting (D) is the hallmark of LMN lesion; hypertonia, absent reflexes, increased reflexes, and Babinski are all UMN characteristics, not LMN.
Syringomyelia characteristically causes bilateral suspended sensory loss for pain/temperature because the central canal syrinx crosses pain fibers first.
Hindbrain excludes crus cerebri because it is a midbrain structure; medulla, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle form the rhombencephalon.
Cerebellum is not part of the brain stem proper, though it connects via peduncles; the brain stem consists only of midbrain, pons, and medulla.
Cranial XI arises from nucleus ambiguus in the medulla and its fibers join the vagus nerve; the spinal part arises separately from C1-C5 levels.
